opus-5.5.text:
Well, this is really the big open question, and I think it's probably the most important challenge in AI for the next few years. We know how to train a world model at one level of abstraction, more or less. That's what JEPA-style architectures are about: you take an observation, say a video, you corrupt or mask part of it, run both through encoders, and train a predictor to predict the representation of the full signal from the representation of the partial one. The key is that you predict in representation space, not pixel space. You don't try to predict every detail, because most details are unpredictable. You let the system learn an abstract representation where prediction becomes possible.

Now, the hierarchical part. If you want to plan complex actions, you can't plan at the level of millisecond-by-millisecond muscle control. If I'm in New York and want to go to Paris, I don't plan my trip in terms of muscle twitches. I plan at a high level: go to the airport, catch a plane. Then I decompose: to get to the airport, I need to get down to the street and find a taxi. And so on, all the way down to "stand up from this chair." Each level has its own representation and its own time scale. Higher levels are more abstract and predict further into the future, but with less detail.

So the question is how to get a system to learn those levels on its own, without us hand-designing what the abstractions should be. The intuition is that you stack JEPAs. The lower level makes short-term, detailed predictions. Its representations feed a higher level that makes longer-term, coarser predictions. The higher level should learn to throw away whatever the lower level can't predict over long horizons, and keep what remains predictable.

But there are real technical problems we haven't fully solved. One is collapse. With joint embedding architectures you have to prevent the system from ignoring the input and producing constant representations, because then prediction is trivially perfect. We have methods for that, contrastive methods, regularization methods like VICReg, distillation tricks, but making them work robustly at multiple levels at once is not obvious. Another is latent variables. The world isn't deterministic, so the predictor needs latent variables representing what you don't know about the future, and you have to regularize them so they don't carry too much information. And then there's how the levels interact during planning, so that a high-level plan sets subgoals that become objectives for the level below. That's essentially hierarchical model predictive control, but learned end to end.

Data matters too. I don't think you get there with text alone. A four-year-old has taken in as much data through vision as the biggest language models are trained on in text, and that sensory data is far richer in information about how the world works. So these systems need to be trained mostly on video, and eventually on interaction, where the system takes actions and observes the consequences. That's how you learn a world model you can actually plan with.

So my guess is that the next steps are: get single-level JEPA world models working really well on video, show that they can be used for planning in robotics and similar settings, which we and others are starting to see, and then find the right training recipe to stack them so abstraction emerges naturally. I don't think it's one breakthrough. It's probably a few good ideas plus a lot of engineering. But I'm convinced this is the path to systems that understand the physical world, have persistent memory, can reason and plan. Not just scaling up autoregressive LLMs, which I think is a dead end for that purpose.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses improving single-level JEPA models on video and stacking them, but does not identify matching existing video-modeling performance as the goal of scaling a preferred small-scale training methodology.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing to say is that we don't have it yet. We have pieces. We have self-supervised learning that works very well for text, because text is discrete and you can predict a distribution over a finite vocabulary. The world is not like that. The world is continuous, high-dimensional, and full of details you cannot predict and should not try to predict. So the whole generative approach, where you reconstruct pixels or predict every detail of the next frame, I think is largely a dead end for learning world models. You spend all your capacity on things that don't matter.

So the direction I've been pushing is joint embedding predictive architectures, JEPA. You take an observation, you encode it into an abstract representation, and you predict the representation of the next state, or of a corrupted or masked version, in that abstract space, not in input space. The encoder is free to throw away the unpredictable stuff. That is really the key idea: prediction in representation space, with the representation learned so that it keeps what is predictable and discards what is noise.

Now, the hard part, and the thing that took us years, is how to train that without collapse. If you just minimize prediction error in embedding space, the trivial solution is to make the embedding constant. So you need either contrastive methods, which I've become fairly skeptical of because they scale badly in high dimension, or regularization methods. VICReg, Barlow Twins, this family of things, where you push the embeddings to have high information content, to be decorrelated, to cover the space. And we have things like I-JEPA and V-JEPA that show this works for images and video. The representations you get are good for downstream tasks, and the models seem to pick up some notion of what is physically plausible without ever generating a pixel.

But that's a single level. The question you're asking is about hierarchy, and that's where it gets interesting and where I honestly don't think we have the answer. The intuition is clear. At the lowest level you predict over short time scales, in a representation that is fairly close to the sensory input. At the next level you want a representation that is more abstract and evolves more slowly, so that you can predict further into the future, but with less detail. You go up the hierarchy and at some point the representation is "I'm going to the airport," and the prediction is at the scale of hours, with all the low-level stuff abstracted away. This is what you need for planning. You cannot plan a trip by predicting every muscle twitch.

How do you train that in a general way? A few ingredients I think are necessary. One, each level should be trained to predict in its own representation space, same principle as JEPA, so the architecture is in some sense recursive. Two, the higher level has to be driven by the lower level's representation but at a coarser time scale, so you need some mechanism for temporal abstraction, and we don't have a clean learned version of that yet. People hand-design it. Three, and this is the part I keep coming back to, the training signal for higher levels probably should not just be prediction. It should be tied to planning. The representation at level k is good if it allows the planner at level k to produce sub-goals that the level below can actually achieve. So there's a coupling between the world model and the cost or the objective that I think has to be learned jointly. Whether that can be done fully self-supervised, or whether you need some reinforcement-like signal at the top, I don't know.

I'll say also that there are a lot of hard questions nobody has really resolved, like how to handle uncertainty properly in the abstract space. The world is not deterministic, so the predictor needs latent variables that capture the things it can't infer from the past, and you need to regularize those latents so the model doesn't just cheat by stuffing the answer into them. Energy-based formulations are, in my view, the right framework to think about all of this, but the practical recipes are still immature.

So the honest answer is: the next steps are, first, make single-level JEPA work really well on video and on robotic interaction data, because that is the foundation. Then stack two levels and get temporal abstraction to emerge rather than be designed. Then connect it to a planner so that the hierarchy is actually used. I think that's a few years of work, maybe more, and I think it's a lot more promising than scaling up autoregressive token prediction and hoping intelligence falls out. That approach has a lot of momentum right now, but I don't think it leads to systems that understand the physical world.

astra-6.text:
I think the first thing is to figure out how to learn representations of the world that make prediction possible. You don’t necessarily want to predict every detail of what’s going to happen. If you’re watching a tree moving in the wind, predicting the exact position of every leaf is both very difficult and mostly irrelevant. You want to predict in a representation space that captures the things that matter, while allowing uncertainty about the rest.

Then you need to do this at multiple levels of abstraction. At a low level, you might predict what happens over a fraction of a second. At a higher level, you might predict the consequences of an action over several seconds, or an entire sequence of actions. The interesting question is how those levels can learn together, so that the higher levels discover useful abstractions rather than having us specify them by hand.

And ultimately, those models have to support planning. Can the system imagine different action sequences, predict their consequences, and choose one that satisfies an objective? That gives us a way to judge whether the representations are useful.

I don’t think we have a complete, general recipe for this yet. We have to solve representation learning, prediction under uncertainty, and hierarchical planning in a way that makes them work together. That’s the research problem.

r003.rationale: It says models should imagine action sequences, predict their consequences, and choose one to meet an objective, describing how action-conditioned models could support planning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the next step is to figure out how to learn representations at multiple levels of abstraction, and then learn to predict in those representations. You don’t necessarily want to predict every detail of the world. If you’re planning a sequence of actions, you need to predict the aspects of the world that matter for those actions, at the appropriate time scale.

So imagine a hierarchy where the lower levels describe relatively short-term, detailed changes, and the higher levels describe more abstract changes over longer periods. The difficulty is getting those levels to emerge through learning, rather than deciding in advance what each level should represent.

There are a few problems we have to solve together. How do you learn useful representations without having them collapse to something uninformative? How do you handle the fact that the future is uncertain? And how do you use the resulting model to plan actions across different time scales?

I don’t think we have a complete, general recipe yet. The important thing is to make these ideas work together in a system that can learn from observations and interactions, and then use what it learns to accomplish new tasks.
